claim: Primary cilia are present on the majority of neurons in the mammalian brain throughout adulthood.
source: Primary cilia are compartmentalized sensory organelles present on the majority of neurons in the mammalian brain throughout adulthood.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by citations in the introduction (Arellano et al., 2012; Guadiana et al., 2016; Sterpka and Chen, 2018).

claim: Acute cell-autonomous knockdown of ciliary signaling rapidly strengthens glutamatergic inputs onto cultured rat neocortical pyramidal neurons.
source: Here we show that acute cell-autonomous knockdown of ciliary signaling rapidly strengthens glutamatergic inputs onto cultured rat neocortical pyramidal neurons and increases spontaneous firing.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Acute knockdown of ciliary signaling increases spontaneous firing in neocortical pyramidal neurons.
source: Here we show that acute cell-autonomous knockdown of ciliary signaling rapidly strengthens glutamatergic inputs onto cultured rat neocortical pyramidal neurons and increases spontaneous firing.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 4A.

claim: The increased excitability from ciliary signaling disruption occurs without changes to passive neuronal properties or intrinsic excitability.
source: This increased excitability occurs without changes to passive neuronal properties or intrinsic excitability.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 3D, 3E, and 4B.

claim: SSTR3 is localized nearly exclusively to excitatory neuron cilia both in vivo and in culture.
source: Further, the neuropeptide receptor somatostatin receptor 3 (SSTR3) is localized nearly exclusively to excitatory neuron cilia both in vivo and in culture
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by immunostaining data in Figure 5.

claim: Pharmacological manipulation of SSTR3 signaling bidirectionally modulates excitatory synaptic inputs onto neocortical pyramidal neurons.
source: pharmacological manipulation of SSTR3 signaling bidirectionally modulates excitatory synaptic inputs onto these neurons
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 6.

claim: Ciliary neuropeptidergic signaling dynamically modulates excitatory synapses.
source: Our results indicate that ciliary neuropeptidergic signaling dynamically modulates excitatory synapses
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the abstract based on the experimental findings.

claim: Defects in ciliary regulation may underlie a subset of behavioral and cognitive disorders associated with ciliopathies.
source: suggest that defects in this regulation may underlie a subset of behavioral and cognitive disorders associated with ciliopathies
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion stated in the abstract based on the findings.

claim: Cilia concentrate signaling molecules and play critical roles in transducing environmental stimuli to regulate cellular properties.
source: Cilia concentrate signaling molecules and play critical roles in transducing environmental stimuli to regulate cellular properties (Bangs and Anderson, 2017; Elliott and Brugmann, 2019; Goetz and Anderson, 2010; Hilgendorf et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Disruption of cilia and cilia-based signaling is causal to a set of pleiotropic disorders termed ciliopathies.
source: Consequently, disruption of cilia and cilia-based signaling is causal to a set of pleiotropic disorders termed ciliopathies (Davis and Katsanis, 2012; Reiter and Leroux, 2017; Youn and Han, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Abnormalities in brain development are a characteristic feature of many ciliopathies.
source: Abnormalities in brain development are a characteristic feature of many ciliopathies, highlighting the critical role of cilia in the nervous system (Guemez-Gamboa et al., 2014; Louvi and Grove, 2011; Valente et al., 2014; Youn and Han, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Cilia have been implicated in neurogenesis, neuronal migration, and establishment of synaptic connectivity during development.
source: Cilia have now been implicated in neurogenesis, neuronal migration, and establishment of synaptic connectivity during development (Baudoin et al., 2012; Chizhikov et al., 2007; Guo et al., 2017; Guo et al., 2019; Higginbotham et al., 2012; Higginbotham et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2020; Spassky et al., 2008; Willaredt et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Cilia along with their complex signaling machinery are retained on mature neurons.
source: Intriguingly, cilia along with their complex signaling machinery are retained on mature neurons (Arellano et al., 2012; Guadiana et al., 2016; Sterpka and Chen, 2018)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Loss of cilia and ciliary signaling results in defects in dendritic development and integration of adult born neurons into hippocampal circuits.
source: Loss of cilia and ciliary signaling results in defects in dendritic development and integration of adult born neurons into hippocampal circuits (Kumamoto et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Disruption of ciliary signaling reduces dendritic complexity and affects synaptic connectivity of interneurons in the postnatal striatum.
source: Disruption of ciliary signaling also reduces dendritic complexity and affects synaptic connectivity of interneurons in the postnatal striatum (Guo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Cilia loss in mature dentate granule cells leads to altered contextual memory and synaptic plasticity at hippocampal mossy fiber synapses.
source: Moreover, cilia loss in mature dentate granule cells leads to altered contextual memory and synaptic plasticity at hippocampal mossy fiber synapses (Rhee et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Cilia in cerebellar Purkinje neurons are necessary for the maintenance of excitatory contacts from climbing fibers.
source: In a particularly interesting study, cilia in cerebellar Purkinje neurons were shown to be necessary for the maintenance of excitatory contacts from the climbing fibers of neurons in the inferior olivary nuclei of the medulla (Bowie and Goetz, 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: The effects on neuronal and circuit properties from cilia loss manifested after prolonged (weeks to months) loss of cilia and/or ciliary signaling in the postnatal brain.
source: In these reports, the effects on neuronal and circuit properties, and on synaptogenesis and synapse maintenance, manifested after prolonged (weeks to months) loss of cilia and/or ciliary signaling in the postnatal brain.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction summarizing previous findings.

claim: Neuronal cilia in different brain regions specifically localize a diverse set of neuropeptide and neurotransmitter receptors.
source: Neuronal cilia in different brain regions specifically localize a diverse set of neuropeptide and neurotransmitter receptors.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by subsequent citations.

claim: Cilia-localized receptors in the brain include serotonin receptor 6, melanin-concentrating hormone receptor 1, somatostatin receptor 3 (SSTR3), and dopamine receptors D1, D2, and D5.
source: Cilia-localized receptors in the brain include serotonin receptor 6, melanin-concentrating hormone receptor 1, somatostatin receptor 3 (SSTR3), and dopamine receptors D1, D2, and D5 among others (Berbari et al., 2008a; Brailov et al., 2000; Domire et al., 2011; Hamon, 1999; Händel et al., 1999; Loktev and Jackson, 2013; Marley and von Zastrow, 2010; Schulz et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Signaling via ciliary receptors is proposed to be mediated in part via regulation of adenylyl cyclase 3 (AC3) and the cAMP second messenger.
source: Signaling via these ciliary receptors is proposed to be mediated in part via regulation of adenylyl cyclase 3 (AC3) and the cAMP second messenger.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is based on established knowledge.

claim: AC3 is specifically enriched in the cilia of diverse neuron types in the brain.
source: Similar to the localization patterns of these receptors, AC3 is also specifically enriched in the cilia of diverse neuron types in the brain (Berbari et al., 2007; Guadiana et al., 2016; Bishop et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Mutations in ciliary receptors and AC3 are associated with a range of cognitive, metabolic, and behavioral disorders that are hallmarks of many ciliopathies.
source: Mutations in these receptors and AC3 are associated with a range of cognitive, metabolic, and behavioral disorders that are hallmarks of many ciliopathies (Chen et al., 2016; Einstein et al., 2010; Lee and Gleeson, 2011; Loktev and Jackson, 2013; Wang et al., 2011; Youn and Han, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Neuronal circuits must maintain excitability within narrow bounds to prevent signal saturation or silencing.
source: Neuronal circuits must maintain excitability within narrow bounds to prevent signal saturation or silencing (Turrigiano and Nelson, 2000)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Several ciliopathies manifest with symptoms consistent with imbalances in excitability, such as cognitive impairment and recurrent epileptic seizures.
source: Several ciliopathies manifest with symptoms consistent with imbalances in excitability, such as cognitive impairment and recurrent epileptic seizures (Guemez-Gamboa et al., 2014; Lee and Gleeson, 2011; Novarino et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Ciliogenesis in neocortical pyramidal neurons occurs progressively during early postnatal development, beginning at birth.
source: Ciliogenesis in neocortical pyramidal neurons occurs progressively during early postnatal development, beginning at birth, with cilia reaching maximal lengths after several weeks (Arellano et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: After 11 days in vitro (DIV), the majority of cortical neurons extended a single primary cilium from their soma.
source: After 11 days in vitro (DIV), the majority of cortical neurons extended a single primary cilium from their soma, as assessed via staining with the neuronal cilia markers ARL13B and AC3 (Figure 1A,B; Berbari et al., 2007; Bishop et al., 2007; Caspary et al., 2007; Sipos et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1A,B and citations.

claim: Approximately 90% of both excitatory and inhibitory neurons exhibited cilia at DIV11.
source: Approximately 90% of both cell types exhibited cilia of lengths similar to those of postnatal neocortical neurons in vivo (Arellano et al., 2012; Figure 1A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1B and a citation.

claim: Cilia lengths varied but were similar across excitatory and inhibitory cell types.
source: Cilia lengths varied as expected (Arellano et al., 2012), but were similar across cell types (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1C and a citation.

claim: Pyramidal neurons transfected with shArl13b for 24 or 48 hr showed a reduction in total immunolabeled ARL13B fluorescence in cilia by ~50%.
source: Pyramidal neurons transfected with either shRNA for 24 or 48 hr showed a reduction in total immunolabeled ARL13B fluorescence in cilia by ~50% as compared to non-transfected control cells (Figure 1D,E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Reduction in ARL13B was sufficient to shorten cilia in postnatal pyramidal neurons.
source: This reduction in ARL13B was sufficient to shorten cilia (assessed using AC3 fluorescence) in these postnatal pyramidal neurons (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), as reported previously in other cell types (Caspary et al., 2007; Cevik et al., 2010; Larkins et al., 2011; Lu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, as well as citations.

claim: Acute and cell-autonomous knockdown of ARL13B for 24 or 48 hr had no impact on the total length of apical-like dendrites or on the number of dendritic branch points.
source: However, in contrast to the significant reduction in dendritic complexity observed upon prolonged conditional Arl13b deletion in striatal interneurons (Guo et al., 2017), acute and cell-autonomous knockdown of ARL13B for 24 or 48 hr had no impact on the total length of apical-like dendrites, or on the number of dendritic branch points (Figure 1G–I, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figures 1G-I and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-E, as well as a citation for comparison.

claim: Co-transfection of shIft88 and shCep164 reduced IFT88 immunofluorescence by ~70% after 48 hr.
source: However, while co-expression of shIft88 and shCep164 reduced IFT88 immunofluorescence by ~30% after 24 hr, co-transfection of both shRNAs reduced IFT88 immunofluorescence by ~70% after 48 hr (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F,H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F,H.

claim: Despite dramatic disruption of cilia structure by shIft88 and shCep164, no gross effects on pyramidal neuron morphology were observed.
source: Despite the dramatic disruption of cilia structure under these conditions, we again observed no gross effects on pyramidal neuron morphology (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-E.

claim: Acute cilia disruption does not strongly impact short-term maintenance of postnatal pyramidal neuron dendritic morphology.
source: We conclude that acute cilia disruption does not strongly impact short-term maintenance of postnatal pyramidal neuron dendritic morphology.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the morphology data.

claim: Manipulation of cilia signaling using shArl13b or shIft88/shCep164 increased the intensity of the surface synaptic GluA2 signal.
source: Manipulation of cilia signaling using either method increased the intensity of the surface synaptic GluA2 signal; this increase was evident at both 24 hr and 48 hr after transfection with shArl13b, and at 48 hr after transfection with shIft88 and shCep164 (Figure 2C)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2C.

claim: Acute and cell-autonomous cilia disruption increases the synaptic accumulation of AMPAR.
source: indicating that reducing ciliary function increases the synaptic accumulation of AMPAR.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the GluA2 intensity data.

claim: Postsynaptic reduction of cilia function with shArl13b_1 increased presynaptic expression of VGlut1.
source: Postsynaptic reduction of cilia function with shArl13b_1 also increased presynaptic expression of VGlut1, although this change was less robust (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Quantification of the density of putative excitatory synapses revealed a significant increase in excitatory synapse density at 48 hr after knockdown.
source: Quantification of the density of putative excitatory synapses along dendritic arbors also revealed a significant increase in excitatory synapse density that was evident at 48 hr after knockdown (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2D.

claim: Acute and cell-autonomous cilia disruption increases both the number of excitatory synapses and the accumulation of synaptic AMPAR.
source: Thus, acute and cell-autonomous cilia disruption increases both the number of excitatory synapses and the accumulation of synaptic AMPAR.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the synaptic data.

claim: Acute cilia disruption had no significant impact on the fluorescence intensities of GAD65 or Gephyrin at inhibitory synapses.
source: we observed no significant change in the fluorescence intensities of either marker after either 24 or 48 hr following transfection with either shArl13b alone or shIft88 and shCep164 together (Figure 2E,F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Inhibitory synapse density was unaltered following acute cilia disruption.
source: Inhibitory synapse density was also unaltered following acute cilia disruption at either time point (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2G.

claim: Under experimental conditions, ciliary signaling acutely regulates excitatory but not inhibitory synapses onto cultured postnatal pyramidal neurons.
source: We infer that under our experimental conditions, ciliary signaling acutely regulates excitatory but not inhibitory synapses onto cultured postnatal pyramidal neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the synaptic data.

claim: Neurons with acutely disrupted cilia had larger AMPAR-mediated mEPSCs compared to transfected controls.
source: Consistent with the increased accumulation of synaptic AMPAR, neurons whose cilia were acutely disrupted had larger AMPAR-mediated mEPSCs compared to transfected controls (Figure 3A, right).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 3A.

claim: Both shArl13b manipulations shifted the mEPSC amplitude distributions toward larger values.
source: Analysis of the cumulative probability distribution function of individual events showed that both manipulations shifted the amplitude distributions toward larger values (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 3B.

claim: mEPSC frequency was not significantly affected by cilia disruption at 24 hr.
source: mEPSC frequency is quite variable in culture and was not significantly affected by cilia disruption at 24 hr (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 3C.

claim: Input resistance and resting potentials were unaltered by cilia disruption.
source: The increase in mEPSC amplitude caused by cilia disruption was not caused by changes in passive electrical properties, as input resistance (which can affect voltage clamp efficacy) and resting potentials (a measure of cell health) were unaltered (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figures 3D and 3E.

claim: Ciliary signaling acts cell-autonomously to rapidly increase excitatory postsynaptic strength.
source: These results indicate that ciliary signaling acts cell-autonomously to rapidly increase excitatory postsynaptic strength.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the mEPSC data.

claim: The distribution of mean firing rates was shifted toward larger values after acute ARL13B knockdown.
source: As expected, we observed a broad distribution of mean firing rates (Trojanowski et al., 2021; Turrigiano et al., 1998); this distribution was shifted toward larger values after acute ARL13B knockdown, such that mean firing rate roughly doubled upon this manipulation (Figure 4A, right).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 4A and citations.

claim: Knockdown of ARL13B had no significant impact on intrinsic excitability.
source: Knockdown of ARL13B had no significant impact on intrinsic excitability (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 4B.

claim: The increase in mean firing rate is likely driven by the increase in number and strength of excitatory synapses.
source: Taken together with the lack of an effect on passive neuronal properties and dendritic arborization, these data show that intrinsic neuronal excitability and morphology are unaffected by acute and cell-autonomous manipulation of cilia. Instead, the increase in mean firing rate is likely driven by the increase in number and strength of excitatory synapses.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the firing rate and synaptic data.

claim: SSTR3 is widely expressed in the brain and is commonly employed as a marker for neuronal cilia.
source: In particular, the somatostatin receptor 3 (SSTR3) is widely expressed in the brain and is commonly employed as a marker for neuronal cilia (Berbari et al., 2007; Guadiana et al., 2016; Händel et al., 1999; Schulz et al., 2000; Stanić et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: Somatostatin is expressed by a subset of cortical interneurons.
source: Moreover, its endogenous ligand somatostatin is expressed by a subset of cortical interneurons (Gonchar et al., 2007; Lee et al., 2010; Xu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: Expression of SSTR3 begins at birth and increases during postnatal development in the rat hippocampus.
source: Expression of SSTR3 begins at birth and increases during postnatal development in the rat hippocampus (Stanić et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: The majority of pyramidal neurons in each cortical layer contained cilia positive for both AC3 and SSTR3.
source: We found that the majority of pyramidal neurons in each cortical layer contained cilia positive for both AC3 and SSTR3, with a small subset of cilia expressing AC3 alone (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 5A,B.

claim: SSTR3 was present in the cilia of many although not all neurons across cortical layers.
source: We found that SSTR3 was present in the cilia of many although not all neurons across layers (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: The majority of NeuN-positive neurons expressed ciliary SSTR3.
source: We noted that while the majority of NeuN-positive neurons expressed ciliary SSTR3 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Fewer than 10% of GAD67-positive neurons in each layer expressed SSTR3.
source: fewer than 10% of neurons that stained weakly with NeuN but were GAD67-positive in each layer expressed SSTR3 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: The cilia of GAD67-positive interneurons retained expression of AC3.
source: The cilia of GAD67-positive interneurons retained expression of AC3 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 5C.

claim: Ciliary SSTR3 localization is restricted largely to cortical excitatory neurons and is present in only a small fraction of inhibitory neurons.
source: These results indicate that ciliary SSTR3 localization is restricted largely to cortical excitatory neurons and is present in only a small fraction of inhibitory neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the SSTR3 expression data.

claim: Only rare (<5%) ciliary SSTR3 expression was observed in inhibitory interneurons positive for PV and SOM.
source: We observed only rare (<5%) ciliary SSTR3 expression in inhibitory interneurons positive for PV and SOM (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Approximately 30% of ARL13B-positive cilia on cultured neurons were also positive for SSTR3 at DIV11.
source: We noted that ~30% of ARL13B-positive cilia on cultured neurons were also positive for SSTR3 at DIV11 (Figure 5E,F)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 5E,F.

claim: The majority of SSTR3-expressing neurons in culture were excitatory, based on the absence of co-staining with GAD67.
source: The majority of SSTR3-expressing neurons in culture were excitatory, based on the absence of co-staining with the inhibitory neuron-specific marker GAD67 (Figure 5E,F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 5E,F.

claim: SSTR3 was specifically localized to cilia in all expressing cells.
source: Importantly, SSTR3 was specifically localized to cilia in all expressing cells (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 5E.

claim: SSTR3 is expressed primarily, if not exclusively, by excitatory neurons in the neocortex, and is localized specifically to their cilia both in vitro and in vivo.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that SSTR3 is expressed primarily, if not exclusively, by excitatory neurons in the neocortex, and is localized specifically to their cilia both in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the SSTR3 localization data.

claim: Manipulating SSTR3 signaling induced bidirectional changes in the intensity of both Shank3 and VGlut1 at colocalized sites that developed over several hours.
source: Manipulating SSTR3 signaling induced bidirectional changes in the intensity of both Shank3 and VGlut1 at colocalized sites that developed over several hours (Figure 6A,B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 6A,B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The SSTR3 antagonist significantly increased synaptic Shank3 and VGlut1 intensity.
source: The SSTR3 antagonist significantly increased synaptic Shank3 (Figure 6A,B) and VGlut1 intensity (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The SSTR3 agonist significantly reduced the fluorescence intensities of both Shank3 and VGlut1.
source: while the SSTR3 agonist significantly reduced the fluorescence intensities of both markers (Figure 6A,B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The SSTR3 agonist significantly reduced the density of putative excitatory synapses.
source: The SSTR3 agonist also significantly reduced the density of putative excitatory synapses, while the effects of the antagonist on synapse density did not reach statistical significance (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 6C.

claim: The first detectable effects of SSTR3 manipulation were evident after 18 hr and were more robust after 24 hr of treatment.
source: We found that the first detectable effects were evident after 18 hr and were more robust after 24 hr of treatment (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 6B,C.

claim: Neither the SSTR3 agonist nor the antagonist altered cilia lengths.
source: Neither the agonist nor the antagonist altered cilia lengths (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Neither the SSTR3 agonist nor the antagonist affected cell viability.
source: or affected cell viability (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: SSTR3-mediated signaling can dynamically regulate excitatory synaptic properties.
source: These results indicate that SSTR3-mediated signaling can dynamically regulate excitatory synaptic properties
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the SSTR3 pharmacology data.

claim: Neuropeptidergic signaling pathway negatively regulates excitatory synaptic strength.
source: and suggest that this neuropeptidergic signaling pathway negatively regulates excitatory synaptic strength.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the SSTR3 pharmacology data.

claim: SSTR3 retained localization to truncated cilia in shRNA-transfected neurons.
source: SSTR3 labeling could be detected in many but not all of the shortened cilia of shRNA-transfected neurons (Figure 6D), indicating that this receptor retained localization to these truncated cilia.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 6D.

claim: The SSTR3 agonist decreased the fluorescence intensity of Shank3 puncta in control (GFP-expressing) neurons.
source: Consistent with our previous data set (Figure 6B), the SSTR3 agonist decreased the fluorescence intensity of Shank3 puncta in control (GFP-expressing) neurons (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 6E.

claim: In neurons with truncated cilia, the intensity of the Shank3 signal was increased.
source: However, in hairpin-expressing neurons with truncated cilia, the intensity of the Shank3 signal was increased (Figure 6E), also as expected (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 6E.

claim: The SSTR3 agonist was not able to reduce Shank3 intensity in neurons with truncated cilia.
source: Finally, the SSTR3 agonist was not able to reduce Shank3 intensity in neurons with truncated cilia (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 6E.

claim: SSTR3-mediated modulation of excitatory synapses likely relies on proper cilia function.
source: Together, these data suggest that SSTR3-mediated modulation of excitatory synapses likely relies on proper cilia function.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the cilia truncation and SSTR3 agonist data.

claim: Cilia play a critical role in the maintenance of neuronal excitability in the postnatal cortex.
source: We show here that cilia play a critical role in the maintenance of neuronal excitability in the postnatal cortex.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion stated in the Discussion based on all the experimental findings.

claim: Acute disruption of ciliary signaling cell-autonomously and rapidly strengthens excitatory synapses onto glutamatergic pyramidal neurons.
source: Acute disruption of ciliary signaling cell-autonomously and rapidly strengthens excitatory synapses onto glutamatergic pyramidal neurons, without affecting inhibitory synapses.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion stated in the Discussion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Neurons with disrupted cilia have more and stronger excitatory synapses, and increased mean firing rates.
source: Consequently, neurons with disrupted cilia have more and stronger excitatory synapses, and increased mean firing rates.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion stated in the Discussion based on the experimental findings.

claim: SSTR3 neuropeptide receptor is selectively localized to the cilia of cortical excitatory neurons.
source: We find that the SSTR3 neuropeptide receptor is selectively localized to the cilia of cortical excitatory neurons
evidence: This is a summary conclusion stated in the Discussion based on the SSTR3 localization data.

claim: Inhibition or activation of ciliary SSTR3-mediated signaling bidirectionally modulates excitatory synapses onto excitatory neurons on rapid hours-long timescales.
source: and that inhibition or activation of ciliary SSTR3-mediated signaling bidirectionally modulates excitatory synapses onto these neurons on similar rapid hours-long timescales.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion stated in the Discussion based on the SSTR3 pharmacology data.

claim: Neuropeptidergic signaling via cilia-localized receptors can dynamically modulate neuronal excitability.
source: Our results indicate that neuropeptidergic signaling via cilia-localized receptors can dynamically modulate neuronal excitability
evidence: This is a summary conclusion stated in the Discussion based on all the experimental findings.

claim: Disorders arising from altered E/I balance in cortical circuits may in part be due to defects in cilia function in the postnatal mammalian brain.
source: and raise the possibility that disorders arising from altered E/I balance in cortical circuits may in part be due to defects in cilia function in the postnatal mammalian brain.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion stated in the Discussion based on the findings.

claim: Acute and cell-autonomous cilia perturbation affects excitatory synapses onto pyramidal neurons, without impacting dendritic inhibitory synapse number, dendritic arborization, intrinsic neuronal excitability, or passive neuronal properties.
source: We find that acute and cell-autonomous cilia perturbation affects excitatory synapses onto pyramidal neurons, without impacting dendritic inhibitory synapse number, dendritic arborization, intrinsic neuronal excitability, or passive neuronal properties.
evidence: This is a summary statement in the Discussion based on the experimental findings.

claim: The rapid ciliary signaling pathway appears to be specific for the regulation of excitatory synapses.
source: Thus, this rapid ciliary signaling pathway appears to be specific for the regulation of excitatory synapses
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion based on the synaptic data.

claim: The net impact of the observed synaptic changes leads to increased firing rates.
source: Nevertheless, the net impact of the observed synaptic changes leads to increased firing rates
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on the firing rate data.

claim: SOM+ interneurons are present throughout cortical layers.
source: SOM+ interneurons are present throughout cortical layers (Urban-Ciecko and Barth, 2016)
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by a citation.

claim: SOM+ interneurons may modulate excitatory neurons via cilia localized SSTR3.
source: suggesting that these interneurons may modulate excitatory neurons via cilia localized SSTR3.
evidence: This is a speculative statement in the Discussion based on the SSTR3 localization and somatostatin expression data.

claim: AC3 is present in the cilia of both excitatory and inhibitory neurons.
source: Since AC3 is present in the cilia of both excitatory and inhibitory neurons, inhibitory neuron cilia are likely to contain a distinct complement of signaling proteins.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on the AC3 staining data.

claim: Neuronal cilia in the brain express Sonic hedgehog (Shh) signaling components, dopamine and serotonin receptor subtypes, as well as subsets of neuropeptide and neurohormone receptors in a brain region- and cell type-specific manner.
source: Neuronal cilia in the brain express Sonic hedgehog (Shh) signaling components, dopamine and serotonin receptor subtypes, as well as subsets of neuropeptide and neurohormone receptors in a brain region- and cell type-specific manner (Berbari et al., 2008b; Brailov et al., 2000; Domire et al., 2011; Green et al., 2012; Hamon, 1999; Händel et al., 1999; Koemeter-Cox et al., 2014; Loktev and Jackson, 2013; Sipos et al., 2018).

claim: Ciliary localization of signaling molecules can be dynamically modulated by extracellular signals.
source: Adding to this complexity, ciliary localization of these molecules can be dynamically modulated by extracellular signals (Bangs and Anderson, 2017; Domire et al., 2011; Green et al., 2016; Nachury, 2018; Najafi and Calvert, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations.

claim: Central neurons likely actively regulate the targeting and localization of ciliary signal transduction proteins as a function of cell type, developmental stage, and context.
source: Thus, as in olfactory neurons and photoreceptors, central neurons likely actively regulate the targeting and localization of ciliary signal transduction proteins as a function of cell type, developmental stage, and context.
evidence: This is a speculative statement in the Discussion based on the known dynamic regulation of ciliary proteins.

claim: Prolonged loss of cilia signaling (weeks to months) in multiple brain regions has been shown to result in defects in the maintenance of dendritic and axonal morphology, loss of both excitatory and inhibitory synaptic connectivity, and neuronal degeneration.
source: Prolonged loss of cilia signaling (weeks to months) in multiple brain regions has been shown to result in defects in the maintenance of dendritic and axonal morphology, loss of both excitatory and inhibitory synaptic connectivity, and neuronal degeneration (Bowie and Goetz, 2020; Guo et al., 2017; Kumamoto et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations.

claim: Loss of ciliary signaling on acute timescales of hours to days in cultured neocortical pyramidal neurons rapidly alters excitatory synaptic properties without any apparent effects on dendritic morphology.
source: In contrast, we find that loss of ciliary signaling on acute timescales of hours to days in cultured neocortical pyramidal neurons rapidly alters excitatory synaptic properties without any apparent effects on dendritic morphology.

claim: Neuropeptidergic signaling via ciliary receptors continuously modulates neuronal excitability in the mature brain.
source: Our results suggest that neuropeptidergic signaling via ciliary receptors continuously modulates neuronal excitability in the mature brain.
